claims.text: The AWSx ELB component provides APIs for provisioning Application and Network Load Balancers and integrates with API Gateway, ECS, Lambda, and VPC.
The example AWSx load balancer listens on port 80 in the account's per-region default VPC using its public subnets, exposing it to the internet.
The `enableHttp2` property enables HTTP/2 on ALBs; HTTP/2 is not supported for NLBs.

To target an EC2 instance, open ingress traffic to the load balancer (explicitly needed for NLB but not ALB), open egress from the EC2 instance for health checks, and attach the target group; the text refers to five steps.
ALBs automatically open ingress traffic to the ports they listen on, whereas NLBs do not.
The Pulumi AWS registry has API docs for ec2 LaunchTemplate at /registry/packages/aws/api-docs/ec2/launchtemplate/ and autoscaling Group.
When the load balancer's target group is passed in an ECS task definition's `portMappings`, AWSx uses that target group to populate the ECS service's load balancer configuration.
The AWSx ECS component (`awsx.ecs` classes) automatically creates the right ingress and egress rules; raw `aws.ecs` requires manual security group management.
The ECS example program exports a stack output named `url` usable via `pulumi stack output url`.
ECS supports both NLB and ALB; ALBs offer two features making them more attractive for ECS: dynamic host port mapping and path-based routing with priority rules.
Pulumi recommends ALBs for ECS services unless a service requires a feature only available with NLBs.
By default an AWSx load balancer is created internet-facing using the VPC's public subnets; setting `internal` to `true` makes it private.
The load balancer accepts explicit subnets via either the `subnets` property (subnet objects) or the `subnetIds` property (subnet IDs).
The `listener` property chooses smart defaults based on whether the listener is created against a load balancer or a target group.
NLBs support protocols TCP, TLS, UDP, TCP_UDP, QUIC, and TCP_QUIC while ALBs support HTTP and HTTPS; NLBs default to TCP and ALBs select HTTP or HTTPS based on port.

The updated AWS documentation links (create-https-listener, listener-authenticate-users, rule-action-types#fixed-response-actions, rule-action-types#redirect-actions, listener-rules) exist and point to the described content.
The target group `deregistrationDelay` range is 0–3600 seconds and the default is 300.
The target group `slowStart` range is 30–900 seconds or 0 to disable, and it is disabled by default.
Target group `stickiness`, if enabled (ALBs only), uses a cookie to route traffic consistently to the same targets.

The target group `targetType` accepts `instance`, `ip`, `lambda`, and `alb`, with default `instance`; IP targets must be within the VPC's private subnet range, RFC 1918 ranges, or RFC 6598 range (100.64.0.0/10).
The health check `interval` range is 5–300 seconds and the default is 30 seconds.
The health check `healthyThreshold` range is 2–10 and the default is 3.
The health check `unhealthyThreshold` range is 2–10 and default is 3; for NLBs it must equal `healthyThreshold`.
The health check `timeout` range is 2–120 seconds; AWS default is 6 seconds for HTTP target groups and 10 seconds for HTTPS, TCP, and TLS target groups.
Health check `path` is ALB only; NLBs only support health checking target availability.
